text:
2 Ontario women sentenced to life in prison for murder of 12-year-old boy in their care

Ontario couple found guilty of boy’s murder, brother’s torture

Critics call for change after death of Indigenous boy in foster care

Ontario's former child advocate says children's aid societies made 'bad decisions' leading up to death of boy

Ten months after Becky Hamber’s and Brandy Cooney’s murder trial began, the focus at their sentencing hearing today was on the young brothers in their care who suffered abuse over a number of years.

The Burlington, Ont., couple were given life in prison with no chance of parole for at least 25 years, which is the automatic sentence for a first-degree murder conviction.

Sentencing “is the end of this case, but not the ending of the memory of L.L. and only the beginning of J.L.'s life,” Justice Clayton Conlan stressed in Milton Superior Court.

Conlan found the pair guilty in May of murdering L.L., who was 12 when he died after being found emaciated in the basement of the couple’s home in 2022. Hamber and Cooney were also convicted of assaulting, confining and failing to provide the necessaries of life to the younger brother, and were sentenced to several years each, to be served concurrent with the life term.

Today's sentencing hearing began with victim impact statements.

Prominent speakers included J.L., the boys’ biological mother and the brothers’ former foster mother.

Now 14, J.L. told the court about how much he missed his big brother. Later, he said he was anxious and scared to be in court, including having to face Hamber and Cooney, but said, "It's good they got what they deserved."

He also spoke of his goal of becoming a lawyer, saying he likes arguing and thinks accused people deserve representation because they aren't all guilty.

Conlan also heard from firefighters still dealing with the trauma of responding to L.L.'s death, teachers and neighbours wondering if they could have done more and family members grieving a boy who will never grow into adulthood.

Hamber and Cooney were allowed to speak as well.

Both maintained their innocence and said justice wasn’t served. Cooney read a poem she wrote from the perspective of L.L., drawing disgusted looks and scoffs from members of the gallery.

Hamber's lawyer, Monte MacGregor, who months ago grilled J.L. as he testified, turned to address the boy at the sentencing hearing.

"I am hopeful and confident that you will flourish going forward," the lawyer said.

Jody Harbour, an advocate with Halton Indigenous group Grandmother’s Voice, says Indigenous people deserve better treatment from the child welfare system.

People are stuck and don’t know what to do, she says, adding bureaucracy has people so confused that they forget basic humanity.

As a non-status urban Indigenous woman, Harbour says she felt for the boys when the judge affirmed he believes they are Indigenous.

Harbour says she hopes the community can heal from this and other injustices.

J.L. has both testified at the trial and today spoke at the hearing about how much he misses L.L.

Outside the courthouse after sentencing, he says he was anxious and scared to be in court today.

About Hamber's and Cooney's sentences, he says, "It's good they got what they deserved."

Life is calm for him now, he notes.

He also spoke of his goal of becoming a lawyer, saying he likes arguing and thinks accused people deserve representation because they aren't all guilty.

"I think there should be better checks on families" in foster care, he says.

Also speaking outside the courthouse is Sara Biasetti, J.L.’s Grade 2 teacher who testified at the trial.

She says Cooney and Hamber took no responsibility and deserve to be imprisoned for life.

MacGregor, Hamber's lawyer, says outside the courthouse that the focus now is on the people who suffered.

He says he doesn't take on appeal cases, but his client would have a right to try to challenge the decisions.

Any possible appeal would look at Conlan’s decision and be a lengthy process, he says, with nothing likely for several years.

MacGregor says Hamber's outspoken remarks denying her guilt and responsibility could potentially harm their chances of parole, but she has the right to share her view.

Carmelo Alfano and Kathi Wilson, Burlington neighbours of Hamber and Cooney, are speaking to reporters outside the courthouse.

Earlier in court, Wilson read the victim impact statement on behalf of the community.

It was "disgusting" to hear the couple describe themselves as victims, Alfano said.

He said he'll hold a fundraiser to help J.L. go to law school.

Some people in court softly applauded as the judge declared the brothers are Indigenous — contrary to claims by Cooney and Hamber.

One person waved and said "bye bye" as police led the couple out of the courtroom.

"I believe J.L.," Conlan says. "These boys, L.L. and J.L., have always been Indigenous."

"That is the end of this case but not the ending of the memory of L.L. and only the beginning of J.L.'s life."

"The life of one young child has been snuffed out at the hands of these offenders," Conlan says, and J.L.'s life has been altered forever.

Conlan's prison sentence for charges related to J.L. are:

These terms are to be consecutive and served concurrently to the life sentences for murder.

The court will give primary consideration to denouncing and deterring child abuse, Conlan says.

"There is no question that L.L. and J.L. were vulnerable persons," he says, as Indigenous boys in the foster care system.

He says aggravating factors in this case include that the offenders abused members of their family, abused children and abused their positions of trust and authority.

He lists other aggravating factors, including that L.L. and J.L. were significantly harmed and prevented from accessing medical care.

"This is a highly aggravating case," he says, with moral blameworthiness of the offenders "as high as could possibly be imagined."
